messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Carmen

Carmen was fifty-five when she came to the clinic, though the wear around her eyes made her look older. She had served in the Army for twelve years, stationed in Iraq during the surge, and had left active duty nearly two decades ago. But the morning she sat across from the therapist, she was still there in some part of herself—still scanning, still braced, still waiting for the next concussion of sound to unmake her.

The attack had happened on a Tuesday in 2005, a convoy run outside Fallujah that should have been routine. Carmen was riding in the third vehicle, and when the IED detonated beneath the second truck, the blast wave threw her against the door hard enough to crack her ribs. She remembered the smell—burning metal and something else, something organic that she had never been able to name. She remembered the ringing in her ears that lasted for days. But when she tried to piece together the sequence of what happened next—whether she had exited the vehicle before or after the second explosion, whether the screaming she heard came from inside or outside the truck—the timeline fractured. The memories felt too large, too extreme to have actually lived through. She would start to explain to her ex-husband what had happened, and halfway through a sentence she would lose the thread entirely, unable to find the words or the order, and he would look at her with a mixture of pity and distance that made her stop trying.

Now, nineteen years later, Carmen worked the morning shift at a Wells Fargo branch in Phoenix, standing behind the counter processing deposits and withdrawals. The job was steady, anonymous, and it paid the bills. But her life had become a series of careful avoidances that she had stopped noticing as avoidance. She did not attend her sister's wedding last year because the invitation mentioned that several family members had recently lost spouses. She did not go to the grocery store at certain times because the texture of the plastic bags—thin, slightly waxy, the way they crinkled under her fingers—triggered something in her chest that she could not quite name, a sensation that shot her back into the vehicle, into the smell and the heat. Loud noises sent her heart into a gallop: a car backfiring, the sound of a heavy door slamming in the back office, even the pneumatic hiss of the bank's security gate closing at the end of the day. Each sound triggered a flood of physical reactivity—her pulse racing, her breath shallow, her hands trembling—and in those moments the fragmented memories would surface unbidden: a flash of the vehicle's interior, a sensation of pressure, the certainty that something catastrophic was about to happen.

The hypervigilance had become her baseline. Carmen was constantly scanning the faces of her customers, watching for signs of threat in the tilt of a jaw, the narrowness of an eye, the way someone's shoulders sat. She monitored the bank's entrance obsessively, noting who came in, how they moved, what they carried. This vigilance fed her appraisals—the conviction that the world was fundamentally dangerous, that people could not be trusted, that nothing she did would ultimately matter. Because the world was dangerous and she could not control it, because the memories were too fragmented and too extreme to feel real, because her body reacted to triggers she could not always predict or avoid, she had come to believe that she could only survive by remaining on guard. The meaning had drained from her life. Her work was a transaction. Her apartment was a bunker. Her relationships had withered because she could not explain herself, could not let anyone close enough to see the fractured thing she had become.

What finally brought her to the clinic was a moment at the bank three weeks ago. A customer had mentioned, in passing, that his daughter had just lost her husband. Carmen had felt the trigger hit immediately—the loss theme, the talk of death and absence—and in response her threat system had ignited. She found herself studying his face with an intensity that must have frightened him, because he had stepped back and asked if she was all right. In that instant, she realized that she had become a person who frightened strangers, who could not hear a simple story of human loss without her body preparing for war. She made the appointment that evening.
